2: A workload in AWS or O C I that holds an access key is a service account with a password that never expires, sitting in a console nobody in identity governance opens.
This module brings those identities under the same rules as the rest of the track.
Each one is listed and joined to a record with two owners and a sponsor.
Every long-lived credential is an exception with a replace-by date.
And every trust is no wider than its workload needs.
The program decided to extend the track to both clouds, and named the tags that join each identity to its record.

4: Unit 1 is what the vendors say.
AWS says to require workloads to use temporary credentials with IAM roles, and where possible not to create access keys at all.
Oracle recommends instance principals, and rotating A P I keys every ninety days or less.
AWS GovCloud isn't commercial AWS: it has one IAM control plane and no global S T S endpoint, no role between a GovCloud account and a standard one, and a root user with no console sign-in.
IAM Roles Anywhere works there, but it can't fetch revocation lists from a certificate, so AWS says to import your C R Ls instead.
In O C I, instance and resource principals act through a dynamic group, which has no permissions until a policy names it.
Auth tokens and customer secret keys never expire.
And Microsoft Learn says Entra accepts tokens from workloads in AWS, signed with R S two fifty-six only.
Whether a GovCloud account's tokens work with Entra hasn't been tested, so the guide uses that path only after a test.
The program's rule follows: every long-lived credential is an exception with a replacement date.
5: Unit 2 is the exports and the join.
Every command in the guide's two export steps is a read.
In AWS, the credential report lists every IAM user, its password and its first two access keys.
It leaves out service-specific credentials and any key beyond the first two, so the export also lists access keys and service-specific credentials.

Then the roles, with their trust policies, the instance profiles, the O I D C providers, and the Roles Anywhere trust anchors, profiles and C R Ls. List users and list roles don't return tags, so the export reads each user's and role's tags too.
In O C I, against the tenancy's home region, it reads the users, each user's credentials, which come back as identifiers, never the secret, the dynamic groups and the policies.
The join is four tags: system I D, owner one, owner two and sponsor.
Each owner gets its own key, because an AWS tag value can't hold a comma or a semicolon.
An identity with no tags or record is an orphan: disable first, then a person acts.
